clue.text: Song-and-dance partner's state

blocks.note: a pal is a friend or partner; the 's is read as 'has' joining the pieces
to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: A dancer's partner is in a bit of a state after a song-and-dance number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Song-and-dance' looks like a stage act, but here it means a fuss; 'state' is a verb, not a condition.
explanation.definitionFit: A song-and-dance is a needless fuss or commotion, the same as a long tiresome bother made over something.

clue.text: So far the riot's developing around the centre of Southwark

indicators.note: something developing is changing its form, so the letters take a new order
the centre of a word is its middle letter, which is all that is kept
around says the shuffled letters wrap themselves round the other piece

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, with the 's dropped as a mere joining 'is'
the fifth of the nine letters of this London borough is its centre

explanation.surface: A news report: the disturbance in Southwark, a London borough, is still building up so far.
explanation.definitionFit: Hitherto is a formal adverb meaning up to this point in time, the same as so far.

clue.text: Squire's wheels?

blocks.note: first meaning: to squire a lady is to accompany her
second meaning: a Ford model, slang 'wheels' being a car

explanation.surface: What sort of car does the country squire drive?
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is', joining the two meanings. The Ford Escort was a very common British family car, and 'wheels' is slang for a car.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb or noun it means accompanying someone as a companion, and it is also the name of a popular Ford car model.

clue.text: Huddled, weapons raised, German called the shots

indicators.note: in a down entry, something raised is read from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: guns are weapons
G is the abbreviation for German
someone who called the shots was in charge, so led

explanation.surface: A wartime scene: troops huddled with guns up while a German officer gave the orders.
explanation.definitionFit: To snuggle is to nestle close for warmth or comfort, so snuggled matches having huddled together.

clue.text: Noble Henry's last becoming girl – or an earlier one?

definitions.note: the Boleyn girl of the novel is Mary; Henry VIII's earlier lover, before her sister Anne

indicators.note: becoming means turning into something else, so these letters change into a new arrangement
last asks for only the final letter of the name before it

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of the king's name

explanation.surface: Henry's latest noble lady replaces a girl he had before.
explanation.walkthrough: The Other Boleyn Girl is a novel about Mary Boleyn, Henry VIII's lover before he married her sister Anne, so either sister fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Boleyn was Henry VIII's second wife, and her sister Mary was his mistress before that, both bearing this surname.

clue.text: Victoria's first seen in shot cerise and navy, for example

indicators.note: first asks for the opening letter of the name before it
shot fabric is woven to shimmer, and something shot is broken up, so the letters are rearranged
seen in says the single letter sits inside the other letters

blocks.note: the opening letter of the queen's name
taken as written, a cherry-red colour

explanation.surface: A fashion note: Victoria shows up in shot silk of cerise and navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot cerise and navy' reads as fabric colours; navy is not a colour here but one of the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: The navy is one of the armed services, so it is an example of a military service.

clue.text: Taking a month off planning Martinmas 6

definitions.note: a cross-reference: the answer to 6 down, a church service

indicators.note: taking a thing away from a word, with the later off, means removing it
off completes the instruction that the month is taken out of the feast's name
planning means arranging things afresh, so the remaining letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, the feast of St Martin
MAR is the short form of March

explanation.surface: Someone takes a month off to organise the church service for the feast of Martinmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Matins is the Anglican morning prayer service, so it is one kind of church service.

clue.text: Aftereffects of Afghan government's retrenchement

definitions.note: plural, while the answer is singular

indicators.note: retrenchment is cutting back, so the outer letters of the phrase are trimmed away to leave the run inside

blocks.note: the run of letters inside these two words, from the end of the first into the second

explanation.surface: The consequences of spending cuts by the government in Afghanistan.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangover is the lingering after-effect of a night's drinking, or more widely any leftover consequence.

clue.text: 6 sounding utterly normal around college

definitions.note: a cross-reference: the answer to 6 down, a church service

indicators.note: sounding means the word is taken as it is pronounced and given another spelling
around says the word for normal is wrapped round the college

blocks.note: utterly is wholly, which is pronounced the same as the word for sacred
common means ordinary or normal
uni is short for university, a college

explanation.surface: A church service that sounds perfectly ordinary, attended by students.
explanation.definitionFit: Holy Communion, the Eucharist, is a principal church service, so it fits as an instance of the service in 6.

clue.text: Sink a performance, admitting bad start in outskirts of Wirral

indicators.note: start asks for just the opening letter of the word before it
admitting means letting in, so the performance takes the letter inside it
the outskirts of a place are its edges, so only the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: the first of the outer letters of the Merseyside peninsula's name
A as written, plus a show, a performance
the opening letter of bad
the last of the outer letters of the peninsula's name

explanation.surface: A show staged on the edge of the Wirral flops after a poor opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like a verb about a failing show; it is the noun. The Wirral is a peninsula near Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: A washbowl is a basin for washing hands and face, which is what a sink is.

clue.text: Utter pain with old shin guard

indicators.note: to utter is to say out loud, so the word is taken by its pronunciation

blocks.note: to pain someone is to grieve them; the spoken word matches the armour

explanation.surface: Groaning in pain with an outdated shin pad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like an adjective meaning complete; it is the verb, saying the word for pain.
explanation.definitionFit: A greave is a piece of medieval armour protecting the lower leg, an early version of a shin pad.

clue.text: Anxious twitch follows introduction of novel currency

indicators.note: follows says the twitch comes after the other pieces in the order
the introduction of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the first letter of novel
the euro is the currency of much of Europe
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: A nervous twitch sets in when a new currency is brought in.
explanation.definitionFit: Neurotic describes someone abnormally worried or anxious, a stronger form of nervous.

clue.text: Anzac regulars billeted in Miss Locket's folly

indicators.note: regular letters are taken at even intervals, here every second one
troops billeted in a house are lodged inside it, so these letters go inside the name

blocks.note: Lucy Locket is the girl of the nursery rhyme who lost her pocket
the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Australian and New Zealand soldiers lodged at a lady's house: what madness.
explanation.walkthrough: Anzac means a soldier of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, which makes 'regulars' look like army regulars.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunacy means extreme foolishness, and folly is likewise foolish behaviour or a foolish idea.

clue.text: I'd so welcome restaging for knockabout shows

indicators.note: restaging puts something on again in a new form, so the letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: the letters of these three words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A theatregoer would love a revival of slapstick farces.
explanation.definitionFit: Low comedy is broad, slapstick humour, so knockabout shows full of pratfalls are examples of it.

clue.text: Conductor of 6 starts to admit laxity with this kind of error

indicators.note: starts asks for the opening letter of each of the next words

blocks.note: a member of the clergy, who leads the church service of 6 down
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A vicar taking a service owns up to slack mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests an orchestra; here it is the one who conducts a service.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerical error is a slip in copying or record-keeping, so the answer names that kind of mistake.

clue.text: OG (not SN) 6?

blocks.note: surface reading: a jumble of letters that seems to say nothing
setter's reading: the even letters of a four-letter tune are O and G, not its odd ones S and N, and that describes a church service

explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: OG are the second and fourth letters of the word for a tune, so 'OG' is that word's even part, giving the name of an evening service.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the Anglican evening prayer service, one of the church services that 6 down points to.

clue.text: For hamstring cold is a blessing in disguise

indicators.note: something in disguise is concealed, so the word lurks within the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the last

explanation.surface: A proverb-like line: catching a cold before a race is a blessing in disguise for an injured athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamstring' looks like the leg muscle; it is the verb meaning to cripple.
explanation.definitionFit: To hamstring is to cripple by cutting a leg tendon, or more widely to hinder, so it means to put out of action.

clue.text: German city church comes into being

blocks.note: Essen is a city in the Ruhr
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church in a German city is founded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes into being' reads as one phrase meaning starts to exist; 'being' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Essence is a thing's fundamental nature, which is what being means in the philosophical sense.

clue.text: Soup pot?

blocks.note: first meaning: a rich creamy shellfish soup
second meaning: unglazed fired pottery

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a pan for soup; the two words are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a creamy seafood soup and unglazed ceramic ware, so a pot can be made of it.

clue.text: Picturesque and unusual antique missing foot

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters fall out of their normal order
in a down entry the foot is the bottom, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A charming, odd old piece of furniture with a leg missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Quaint means attractively old-fashioned, so it is close to picturesque in describing a charming scene.

clue.text: Everything there is unsettling in revues

indicators.note: unsettling something disturbs it, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A theatre critic finds everything in variety shows disturbing.
explanation.definitionFit: The universe is all existing matter and space considered as a whole, literally everything there is.

clue.text: Invest nearly everything at the end of the month

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is cut
at the end of places this piece after the other one

blocks.note: inst., short for instant, means of the current month in old business letters
all is everything

explanation.surface: Putting nearly all your money in at the end of the month.
explanation.walkthrough: INST. is old commercial shorthand for 'this month'; the answer is the less common one-L spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest someone is to install them formally in an office, as a bishop or knight is installed.

clue.text: Sausage I'm regrettably taking back …

indicators.note: taking back means retracting, so the words run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
alas expresses regret, like regrettably

explanation.surface: A sausage apology: sadly, I'm withdrawing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a highly seasoned Italian sausage, usually eaten cold in slices.

clue.text: … repeated problem with stone inside

indicators.note: a problem means something has gone wrong, so the letters are out of place

blocks.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: Following the previous clue: the sausage keeps coming back, as if a stone were stuck inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' looks like a container signal; it is fodder, along with the weight abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To insist is to say something again firmly, so insisted can mean repeated in the sense of repeatedly stated.

clue.text: Scheme isn't largely captivating team's top banana

indicators.note: largely means mostly but not wholly, so the final letter goes
the top of a word is its first letter
captivating means holding captive, so the letters take the other one inside

blocks.note: a plan is a scheme
ain't is the informal form of isn't
the first letter of team

explanation.surface: A scheme that isn't really winning over the team's star player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top banana' reads as slang for the boss, but 'top' belongs to the wordplay and banana alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plantain is a starchy cooking banana, grown widely in the tropics.

clue.text: Application reviewed in camera, with setter removed

indicators.note: reviewed suggests looking again from a new angle, so the letters are rearranged
removed says the piece is taken out of the phrase

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: A legal application is heard privately, in camera, without the setter present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Application' suggests a court request heard in private; it is something rubbed on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnica is a herbal cream applied to bruises, so it is an application in the sense of something put on the skin.
